Subject: Post-call recap: Performance SLOs & Autoscaling (Acme Retail)

Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks again for the time today — good conversation and helpful context on your production goals. Quick recap and the asks we discussed so we can line up the tech benchmark and sizing: 

Summary of your target SLOs (as I understood them):
- P95 latency for streaming responses: target <= 250ms for ~512-token responses (chunked streaming)
- Sustained concurrency: ~50 concurrent requests (steady state)
- Burst capacity: handle up to 300 concurrent requests for ~2 minutes during peak campaigns
- Streaming: clients consume partial tokens as they arrive; low tail latency on first-token is important

Questions / clarification items for benchmark & sizing:
1) Can you share a 24h traffic distribution (qps by minute/5m) and typical request sizes (avg tokens in/out + peak token sizes)?
2) Is 250ms P95 a hard requirement, or can we design for p95 <= 350ms with automatic routing to a higher-capacity variant on peaks?
3) Any constraints on queued requests (max queue wait before client-side retry or shedding)?
4) Are you planning to run model A (open-llm-v2) or the smaller ensemble variant we demo'd?

What we propose next:
- Please fill the attached SLO template with your current traffic profile and confirm the exact p95 target. (attached: redwood-inference-slo-template.xlsx)
- We'll schedule a 2–3 hour performance run from our dedicated staging pool to validate scale-up times and warm-pool sizing. Neha will own the benchmark and will need the sample payloads.
- We'll include a proposed autoscaling policy (warm pool + reactive scale-up) and an architecture diagram for your infra (attached: architecture-diagram.png).

On autoscaling specifics: high-level notes from today — our typical approach to meet low tail latency and burstiness is:
- Maintain a modest warm pool of pre-warmed workers to serve initial spikes (size tuned to expected bursts)
- Reactive scale-up to the required capacity; we measure scale-up time from decision -> fully ready GPU exec (typical baseline ~30–60s depending on instance type and image pull)
- Queueing: short queue windows (30–90s) are allowed for controlled bursts; beyond that we recommend shedding/fallback to a cheaper model variant or returning a 503 to the client.

I'll follow up with a calendar invite for a benchmark window once we get the filled template.

Best,

Marissa — thanks for the clear recap. A few clarifications from our side: 

- We can confirm the P95 requirement is tighter than I initially said: goal is P95 <= 200ms for most conversational flows (256 tokens), but we can accept <=300ms for the very long (>1024 token) generation paths.
- Sustained concurrency is closer to 80 req/s for peak business hours; average over 24h is ~12 qps.
- Burst: we see short flash traffic up to ~350 concurrent requests for ~3 minutes (marketing push).
- Queueing: client can't tolerate >60s wait for first token. If queueing occurs we prefer automatic fallback to a lightweight summarization model (lower cost) rather than dropping requests.

I'll pull together the traffic profile CSV (we have 1-minute granularity) and the sample payloads for the benchmark. Timeline: procurement is light; happy to run a test week of Feb 22 if you can provision the staging pool by then.

Alex / Team — quick technical follow-up from our side to make sure the benchmark targets are aligned: 

1) Streaming & first-token latency: is the 200ms P95 requirement focused on first-byte/first-token, or end-to-end completion? If it is first-token, we will size warm pools differently to prioritize low cold-start tail.
2) Warm pool expectations: our conservative estimate to hit ~200ms P95 for 256-token streaming on the model you mentioned is ~30–40 pre-warmed workers (dependent on instance type and quantization). We can run a calibration test to confirm.
3) Scale-up / provisioning: our measured cold-start -> ready GPU (image + model load) is ~25–60s depending on image cache + model size. To reduce this we can:
   - Keep a configurable warm pool (pre-loaded model)
   - Use lighter-weight model variant as an automatic fallback
   - Maintain a small reserve of burst-only nodes (charged as burst capacity) to shave the initial seconds off scale-up
4) Queueing policy: we recommend a soft queue cap of ~60–90s with fallback after that window.

We're attaching a filled SLO grid (starter values) and will use your traffic CSV to tune the warm pool size for the Feb 22 run. Neha will reach out to coordinate payload formats and test scripts.

Rishi Malhotra
Account Executive | Redwood Inference

Agreed targets for the POC benchmark (Feb 22):
- Goal: P95 first-token <= 250ms for 256-token streams; p95 <= 350ms for >1024 tokens.
- Sustained concurrency: tune to 80 req/s for peak windows.
- Burst capacity: support up to 350 concurrent for up to 3 minutes with automatic fallback to light variant after 60s queue.

Preliminary sizing and operational plan:
- Warm pool: provision 40 pre-warmed workers for the POC (we'll tune after the calibration run).
- Scale-up time target: instrumented target <= 30s to warm additional nodes (best-effort; depends on instance cache).
- Queue behavior: soft queue up to 60–90s, after which requests are routed to fallback model. We will expose queue metrics in the Console dashboard so you can set client-side retry windows.
